title: Quorum Sensing and Cell Communication
markdown:
## What this covers

This is a short, transitional lecture. It marks the point in the course where the framing moves
from the single cell to the multicellular organism, and it names the experimental system —
quorum sensing in bacteria — that the course uses to study communication between cells. It
assumes the two earlier framings the course had already built: the single cell treated as a
well-stirred reactor, and the role of diffusion and gradients inside a single cell.

## Three framings of systems biology

The lecture organises the course, retrospectively, into three levels, each defined by what it
takes as the unit of study:

| Level | Question |
| --- | --- |
| Systems Microbiology | the single cell as a well-stirred bio-reactor |
| Systems Cell Biology | the importance of diffusion and gradients for cellular regulation in a single cell |
| Systems Developmental Biology | how to build a multicellular organism from single cells — cell-cell communication |

The first two levels treat a single cell as the object of study, differing only in whether its
internal spatial structure matters. The third level is a genuine change of scale: the object of
study becomes a population of cells, and the new ingredient that makes a population behave as
more than a collection of independent cells is communication between them.

## Quorum sensing as the experimental system for cell-cell communication

The lecture introduces quorum sensing in bacteria as "a tractable experimental system for
cell-cell communication" — the system the course uses to make the third level concrete. It names
**N-acyl-L-homoserine lactones (AHLs)** as the main signalling molecules involved. Beyond the name
of the signal, the source does not give the mechanism: the slides carrying the actual diagrams of
the quorum-sensing pathway were images, and both the images and any spoken description of them
are unavailable here (see Sources). So this chapter can record that quorum sensing was the
chosen example and AHLs were the chosen signal, but not reconstruct how the pathway works.

## A worked example: engineering a communication circuit

The lecture points to a specific engineered system as an example of designing cell-cell
communication rather than only observing it:

> You, L., R. S. Cox 3rd, R. Weiss, and F. H. Arnold. "Programmed population control by
> cell-cell communication and regulated killing." *Nature* 428, no. 6985 (22 Apr 2004): 868–71.

As with the quorum-sensing mechanism above, the figure illustrating this circuit was not
recoverable, so only the citation — not the design of the circuit itself — is in the source
available for this chapter.

## Sources

Everything above comes from a single slide file with no accompanying transcript, notes, or
exercises: `computational-biology/mit-ocw/8591j/2004/lectures/23-notes.md` (lecture 23, "23
notes"). That file is itself a model's reconstruction of a PDF with no text layer, and several of
its slides were images "removed due to copyright considerations" — those slides (the quorum-sensing
diagram, the AHL structure diagram, and the figure from You *et al.*) could not be reconstructed
and are not included here.

Omitted from this chapter: administrative announcements at the top of the source (a correction to
question 2(a) of the final problem set, changes to the Tuesday lecture and Wednesday recitation,
and a note that the following Thursday's lecture — on modeling *Drosophila* development — would
be the course's last). These are logistics for the 2004 offering of the course, not material for
a reader learning the subject now.
